text: Chapter 5, consistent hashing. Let's see how it works in a couple of minutes.
Say we spread data across several machines. For every key, we must pick a machine. The simplest way: hash the key, then take the remainder when dividing by N, the number of servers.

With a fixed number of servers, this works fine. But add one machine, and N goes from four to five. Now most keys map somewhere new. The cache misses almost everywhere, every request hits the database, and scaling out causes an outage first.
Consistent hashing takes a different approach. It joins the two ends of the hash space into a ring. Each server is hashed, and lands at one position on that ring.
A key is hashed too, and lands on the ring. From there, walk clockwise. The first server you meet owns that key. If you pass the end, you simply wrap around.
Now add a new server, s4. Only the keys between s4 and the server just before it move over to s4. Everything else stays exactly where it was.
Removing a server works the same way. Its keys all go to the next server clockwise. No other key is affected.
But server positions on the ring are random, so the gaps are uneven. Some machines get a huge slice of the ring, others get only a sliver.
The fix is virtual nodes. Each physical machine takes many positions on the ring. The more positions each one has, the closer every machine gets to an equal share.
One thing to remember: even data is not even traffic. A single hot key still lands on just one machine. That needs cache replication, or splitting the key, to solve.
Remember three words: ring, clockwise, virtual nodes. Systems like Dynamo, Cassandra, and Discord use ideas like this.
